extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent applicants and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and substantive criteria for determining whether patent claim language is definite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA 112 second paragraph), including claim construction (BRI), means-plus-function analysis, examiner recordkeeping, interviews, and correspondence between claims and specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (35 U.S.C. 112(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph) requires that a patent application conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor regards as the invention; claim language must be 'definite' to comply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that do not meet this standard must be rejected as indefinite; such a rejection requires that the examiner identify the indefinite language and thoroughly explain the reasoning so the applicant may amend or explain why the language is definite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary and secondary purposes of definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary purpose: ensure the scope of the claims is clear so the public is informed of the boundaries of infringement. Secondary purpose: provide a clear measure of what the inventor regards as the invention so patentability and written description can be assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examination should focus on these notice and measurement functions when evaluating claim language. Rejections should be tied to failure to meet these purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give claims their Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) consistent with the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination, a claim must be given its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI reduces the chance a claim will later be interpreted more broadly than justified. Words must be given plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification. See MPEP § 2111 and cited case law (e.g., Yamamoto, Zletz, Buszard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain meaning and specification as best source
rubrics_metrics.description: Under BRI, words of the claim must be given their plain (ordinary and customary) meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention, with the specification being the best source for determining meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption of plain meaning can be rebutted only by a clear specification definition. Avoid importing limitations from preferred embodiments absent clear disclaimer. Applicant may not add a special definition after the filing date, though they may point to a special definition present in the specification as filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether each limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means-plus-function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should determine whether each limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph). If invoked, the limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2181 and In re Donaldson. When a limitation invokes 112(f), identify corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification during claim interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different construction for claims in prosecution vs. in court
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims under examination are construed under BRI by the Office, while patented claims in court are not given BRI and are interpreted based on a fully developed prosecution record (Nautilus standard of reasonable certainty applies in litigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should apply a lower threshold for ambiguity during prosecution to facilitate sharpening/clarifying claims; applicants have opportunity to amend during prosecution to ensure clarity prior to issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold requirements: clarity and precision (particularity and distinctness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner’s focus is whether the claim meets statutory threshold requirements of clarity and precision—claims must set out and circumscribe a particular subject matter with reasonable clarity and particularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should allow claims that define patentable subject matter with required particularity even if alternate phrasing exists. Examiners may suggest language improvements but should not insist on personal preferences if statutory requirements are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the evidence: analyze claim terms in light of specification, prior art, and POSITA understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Definiteness must be analyzed in light of (A) the content of the particular application disclosure, (B) teachings of the prior art, and (C) the claim interpretation that would be given by one of ordinary skill in the pertinent art at the relevant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the claim as a whole to determine whether it apprises POSITA of its scope and serves the notice function. A term’s commonly understood meaning may vary by art; analyze from the relevant-art perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness: more than one reasonable interpretation under BRI
rubrics_metrics.description: If the language of a claim, given its broadest reasonable interpretation, is such that a person of ordinary skill would read it with more than one reasonable interpretation, then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse breadth with indefiniteness: a broad but clearly defined claim is not indefinite. Example: a genus claim can be broad yet definite; a genus claim is indefinite if it is unclear which species are covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid per se rules; indefiniteness determinations are fact-specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Office policy is not to employ per se rules to make technical rejections; examples of language held indefinite are fact specific and should not be applied as blanket rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply case-specific reasoning; consult MPEP § 2173.05(d) for examples but do not treat them as automatic tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must establish a clear record when asserting indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as prima facie indefinite, the examiner should clearly communicate findings and reasons supporting the rejection and avoid mere conclusory statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed explanations in the Office action so the file history accurately reflects the basis for the action (see MPEP § 1302.14, § 707.07(f), § 706.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action must provide sufficient explanation for applicant to respond
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office action must set forth the specific term or phrase that is indefinite and why the metes and bounds are unclear, and, when practicable, indicate how the indefiniteness may be resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the rejection requires a response explaining why the language is definite or amending the claim, give enough information for a meaningful response; if applicant fails to adequately respond, the examiner may make the rejection final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide claim interpretation in reasons for allowance when the prosecution record is unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 37 CFR 1.104(e), if the prosecution record as a whole does not make clear the reasons for allowing a claim, the examiner may set forth such reasoning in reasons for allowance (and specify allowable subject matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setting forth reasons for allowance improves the quality and reliability of issued patents but avoid placing unwarranted broad or narrow interpretations on the claims in doing so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt resolution through interview before rejecting when indefiniteness is sole issue
rubrics_metrics.description: When indefiniteness is the only issue, examiners are encouraged to initiate an interview with the applicant to discuss claim interpretation, meaning of limitations, scope of preamble, means-plus-function issues, etc., prior to issuing a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews can clarify issues and may eliminate need for rejection. The substance of any interview must be made of record (document why a term is or is not clear, whether it invokes 112(f), and any amendments discussed). See MPEP § 713.04 and 37 CFR 1.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence between specification and claims; antecedent basis and support (37 CFR 1.75(d)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should serve as a glossary to claim terms so meaning can be ascertained; claim terms must find clear support or antecedent basis in the specification per 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glossaries are helpful. If the specification lacks needed support or antecedent basis, object under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) and require amendment to description or claims (without introducing new matter). See MPEP § 608.01(o) and § 2181 subsection IV.
